I had the pleasure this weekend to try Bohea, a very delicious tea from the Wuyi Mountains of China. This is the same region that my prevailing favorite- Lapsang Souchong- hails. Like Lapsang, there is a smokiness to Bohea, but it is much MUCH more subtle. Others describe it as a fruity aromatic tea. I can't really qualify to that extent, but suffice to say it's delicious.

Loose leaf runs a bit pricey, but can be found for a reasonable $20/lb by Oliver & Co. Disclaimer: I know nothing of the quality of that company. Harney & Sons, whose Lapsang isn't my favorite, also carries the tea but a much more premium price. I do like other teas that Harney & Sons sells.

The history of the tea is quite fascinating! It was one of the most prominent teas of the Colonial era and the largest victim of the Boston Harbor rebellion. [Source]

I live in Norway. I would say that I enjoy living here tremendously, but wouldn't necessarily say that it's the greatest place to live - I've been a bit around the world and there are lots of great places with great people. But, here are some opinions of mine:

  • 6 months of little sun, the summers consists of around 20-25 celcius degrees and often rainy or cloudy weather.
  • The nature is awesome, but you've got awesome nature almost everywhere in the world, so it doesn't really count.
  • People are the same here as people everywhere. Some are good, others are bastards.
  • Some people have got a superiority complex because of being Norwegian. This can be felt often when you're out on the pubs and so forth (mainly in the bigger cities).
  • I like our health care, but it's too bad that dental care isn't provided the same way.
  • Alcohol and tobacco is expensive. We usually go to Sweden, Denmark or Germany to buy it cheaper.
  • I like that we can travel to other countries and experience their culture without having to pay too much (compared to what we would have to pay in Norway).
  • Compared to countries as the US, England and so on we aren't that great with animal laws. We haven't got animal police or anything, although many wants it.

But yeah - Norway is all right.

Gezellig. It's a Dutch word that has no translation in any other language. It roughly means coziness or togetherness, but its meaning goes way beyond that. This website captured it spot on:

A brown café is gezellig. A dentist’s waiting room is not — though it can be gezellig if your friends accompany you, particularly if they are gezellig.

An evening on the town with friends is gezellig, especially if you have dinner at a gezellig restaurant, see a good movie, and finish with a drink at a gezellige pub. Trying to entertain the inlaws-from-hell is definitely not gezellig. Old-fashioned shops and boutiques are gezellig; modern warehouses are not.

Watching a movie at home in a gezellige living room (read: warm colors, warm ambiance, full of books, plants, and knick-knacks, along with a dog or cat or two) is gezellig, especially if you have gezellige friends over. Eating dinner at MacDonald’s is ongezellig — though here again gezellige friends can make a difference.
